To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the solvation parameter models can be used to predict retention in SFC for pharmaceutical compounds; (b) the retention variance can be reduced by adding the D(+) or D(-) terms to the model; (c) the D(+) term is statistically significant for basic compounds; and (d) the D(-) term is statistically significant only for the polar stationary phases and not for the aromatic stationary phases.

the solvation parameter models and their adaptations are inadequate to account for 1) the ionic interactions when describing the chromatographic behavior of pharmaceuticals in supercritical fluid chromatograpy and 2) the variance of retention data when characterizing stationary phase in supercritical fluid chomatography.

the retention of pharmaceuticals on polar and aromatic stationary phase in SFC can be described with a LSER model, that the addition of the ionization terms to the model improves the fit, and that the statistical significance of these terms indicates that ionic interactions play an important role in the retention of ionic compounds.
In summary, our research is concerned with

a more detailed understanding of the retention mechanism in SFC and the development of a model that can be used for stationary phase characterization and prediction of the retention behavior of pharmaceutical compounds.

the development of an adequate model to describe retention of pharmaceutical compounds with different charge states in SFC, and the results indicate that the LSER models with ionization terms are adequate.
the characterization of SFC columns and with the development of a model to predict the retention of pharmaceutical impurities on SFC columns.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the LSER approach is a useful and valuable method for characterizing stationary phases, but the models obtained should be used with caution.
the LSER approach can be applied to SFC but the models are less predictive than in HPLC and the D(+)D(-) terms are not necessary for the characterization of the stationary phase.
the LSER model is adequate to account for ionized compounds when characterizing stationary phase for drug impurity analysis by SFC.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the solvation parameter models, with and/or without the D(+) or D(-) terms, are adequate to characterize SFC stationary phases for pharmaceutical impurity profiling, but the models do not explain the variance of the retention data completely.
the solvation parameter models, with and/or without the ionization descriptors, are useful tools for the characterization of stationary phases and prediction of retention of pharmaceutical compounds.
the solvation parameter models are adequate to characterize stationary phases for drug profiling with SFC.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the retention models for SFC, as well as for LC, should be modified by the D(+) or D(-) terms to account for the influence of ionic interactions.

the retention models obtained for the SFC stationary phases were comparable to those obtained for liquid chromatographic stationary phases, and that the retention mechanisms in SFC and HPLC are very similar.

the LSER approach is a valuable tool to describe the retention behavior of pharmaceutical compounds in supercritical fluid chromatograph, but it is not sufficient to characterize the stationary phases.
